title: BBR-TAS: A TSQ-Adaptive Pacing Shift Design for BBR-v3 over Wi-Fi 6 Networks
content: Wi-Fi 6 has emerged as the ubiquitous wireless standard providing ample radio bandwidth at the client side. To unleash this bandwidth, Google’s algorithms TCP Small Queues (TSQ) and TCP Pacing play an important part. They were introduced to mitigate bufferbloat on the client side, but their default configurations limit the frame aggregation that is needed for Wi-Fi 6 to provide optimal throughput. Google’s modern model-based congestion control algorithm, Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time (BBR), which performs well on wired links, has shown limitations over wireless links, as its default fixed pacing shift is not sufficient to provide enough frames to the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer for aggregation purposes. This paper proposes BBR-TAS (TSQ-Adaptive Shift), a BBR-v3-based congestion control algorithm that modifies the pacing shift across the Startup and Steady-state phases of BBR to ensure enough frames are delivered to the TCP connection to perform optimum frame aggregation. We have evaluated BBR-TAS against BBR-v3 and TCP CUBIC on a physical Wi-Fi 6-based testbed running a Linux kernel for both client and server. Rigorous testing via the Flent network testing tool to measure throughput, induced latency, and TCP RTT across various pacing shift combinational configurations under both single-flow upload and Realtime Response Under Load (RRUL) strenuous conditions. Our results showed that BBR-TAS achieves a 11% and 9% decrease in latency as compared to CUBIC and BBR-v3, respectively, in single-flow upload tests. Under the RRUL test, BBR-TAS achieved a 13% increase in throughput as compared to BBR-v3 and a major latency improvement of ~59% over CUBIC and ~15% over BBR-v3. BBR-TAS outperforms other congestion controls (CC) in the RTT_Fair test, with a 14.58% reduction over CUBIC (180 ms) and a 41.2% reduction over BBR-v3 (261.5 ms).
